items_missed: No agenda statement. He asked permission — 'is now an okay time to chat about the details of your move' — but never set the roadmap or the timeframe ('I'll gather some details, then walk you through pricing, about 10-15 minutes'), so Leslie never knew the call had a pricing segment coming.

Never checked availability for the move date. He asked 'do you have flexibility on your move date or is September 11th kinda like a firm date' purely to set up the day-of-week rate pitch — he never confirmed Einstein actually has crews open on the 11th, the 10th, or the Sunday he quoted.

Told the customer she was disqualified before checking scope: 'we're not able to move refrigerators up or downstairs for liability reasons. Unfortunately, we wouldn't a good fit for this project.' Leslie had to rescue the job herself — 'Are you able to do the other things or just not the fridge?' — before he corrected to 'Yeah, we can move the other stuff.' One sentence nearly ended a bookable move.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned — the largest miss on the call. Leslie volunteered exactly the setup for it: 'there is a Carrio [curio] cabinet that... I would say is delicate and then, there is a granite marble... slab so that's a table.' Two named fragile specialty items and no coverage story.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener — he led with the mechanic instead ('we're an hourly rate company we charge $206 an hour').

No what's-included list. He covered what they don't charge for ('no hidden fees, so you don't have to worry about gas charges, fuel charges, credit card charges') but never named what the rate does include — truck, taxes, insurance, wrap, pads, bands, tools.

Disassembly / reassembly never mentioned, on a job whose entire inventory is furniture: 'a dining room table... some dressers... a TV stand... I think there's two book cases.' The one service most likely to matter here went unpitched and unpriced.
Clock start never explained — no 'the clock starts on-site when we open the contract,' which matters on a two-address move with a ten-minute drive between them.

No sense-check anywhere in the pricing or clock walkthrough — no 'does that make sense?' after quoting $206/hr, the 2.5-hour minimum, the $515 out-the-door, and three separate day-tier prices back to back.

Estimate leans on the minimum against the physical facts of the job. He concluded 'I anticipate that two and a half hour minimum could be realistic for your project' for a stairs carry of a dining table, a curio cabinet, dressers, a TV stand, two bookcases and a marble sofa table down a flight of stairs from a second-floor unit, plus a ten-minute drive and a full unload. No typical time range for the home size was given, and stairs, specialty handling and drive time were never named as time drivers.

Box count was assumed, not asked: 'we're not anticipating taking any boxes or tow. So, I'll kind of keep it a lower number... I'll put in there about ten.' He set the number himself and Leslie only said 'Mm-hmm' — that is an unverified input feeding the estimate.
Never asked about packing needs, storage stops, additional stops, garage/balcony/storage-unit contents, or parking/HOA access at either address.

Never asked the moving-stressor question. Leslie twice signalled the real concern — 'there is just things that we need to help getting down the stairs' and 'the bigger furniture items is what we really need to help with' — and it was never named back to her or noted for the crew.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. Leslie handed him the opening: 'There will be other things in the apartment like from totes and stuff that we can do.' She was already self-prepping and he never reinforced it with prep-equals-shorter-move-equals-lower-bill, consolidation examples, or the take-a-carload tip — on a call where the whole bill hinges on beating a 2.5-hour minimum.

No 'no deposit required.' Leslie's one hesitation was commitment risk ('does that like kind of change or I just call if I want to book it') and the answer to that hesitation is Einstein's no-deposit policy. He answered the rate-lock half and skipped the deposit half.

Booking attempt offered the customer the exit: 'did you want to go ahead and get booked for this or did you want me to send you over this estimate for you to review?' She took the review option, and he accepted it with no attempt to hold the date.

No BOLDED-details framing for the confirmation email and no 'reply with any corrections' — notable because the estimate carries an assumed 10-box count and a fridge exclusion that Leslie should be verifying in writing.
Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?' and never gave hours or how to reach us, even though Leslie explicitly said she would 'just call if I want to book it.'
Customer's name used once — 'Hey, Leslie, this is Dustin' — short of the 3+ standard (the second occurrence is only him reading her email address back).
top_strength: Dustin ran a genuinely well-prepared, efficient discovery. He had the quote form in front of him and confirmed every detail out loud instead of guessing — the origin ('that's a 900 square foot second floor unit'), the destination ('518 Brisbane drive in Selma... that's a one story house about 1200 square feet'), and walk distance at both ends — and he asked the specialty-items question in the right, concrete form: 'do you have any special considerations for your move? These are usually heavier things like safes and pianos or delicate things like antique or a glass, or marble furniture,' which is precisely what surfaced the curio cabinet and the marble table. He also caught the partial-move note on the form and chased it down rather than quoting a full 900 sqft apartment. The standout is unprompted budget-conscious selling: he volunteered the day-of-week tier without being asked — 'Fridays and Saturdays we have our standard pricing and then the other days of the week or a slightly lower rate' — then priced the alternatives concretely ('that hourly rate drops down to $192 for September 10th and you'd be looking at $480'), and he pre-empted the rate-risk objection cleanly: 'The pricing won't change. This will be attached to your profile. So, even if we raise the rates tomorrow, yours will be locked in.' That is a real, customer-first FAQ answer delivered before it became an objection.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix is the disqualification reflex. Dustin heard 'refrigerator' and said 'we wouldn't a good fit for this project' — he walked away from the whole move over one item, and only Leslie asking 'Are you able to do the other things or just not the fridge?' saved it. The line he needed, immediately: 'Leslie, the one thing we can't do is take a fridge up or down stairs — that's a liability rule on our end. Everything else on your list is exactly what we do, so let's get the dining table, the dressers, the bookcases and that marble table covered and you can handle the fridge separately. Sound good?' Scope the exclusion, never the customer. Second: she named two fragile specialty items in one breath and got no coverage story. He should have said 'That curio cabinet and the marble slab table are exactly why we carry No Worries Damage Coverage — up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse accidental damage, and I'm noting both on your job so the crew brings extra pads and blanket-wraps them before they touch the stairs,' then rolled straight into Meet Your Mover and the On-Time Guarantee. Three differentiators, zero hits, on the one call where the customer pre-sold the need for them. Third, and this is the estimate-accuracy one: he anchored the whole quote on the 2.5-hour minimum ($515 out the door) for a second-floor stairs carry of a dining table, curio cabinet, dressers, a TV stand, two bookcases and a marble sofa table, plus a ten-minute drive and a full unload — with a box count he set himself at ten without confirming it. The honest framing is 'moves like this usually run three to three and a half hours once we account for the stairs carry and the drive, so plan on the $618 to $700 range and anything under that is money back in your pocket.' Under-anchoring on the minimum is how a $515 promise becomes a $700 invoice and a bad move-day conversation. Finally, the Save Your Ass speech was free money here and he skipped it: Leslie said out loud she'd move the totes herself, which is the perfect cue for 'That's exactly the right instinct — every box and loose item you get out ahead of us is time off the clock, and at $206 an hour that's real money. Anything small enough for a carload, take it. Does that make sense?' On a job priced at a 2.5-hour minimum, that speech is the difference between hitting the minimum and blowing through it.
phone_presence_notes: Organized, upbeat and easy to follow, but the warmth is filler rather than connection — 'Awesome,' 'Perfect' and 'Gotcha' appear more than a dozen times as transitions while Leslie's actual concern ('things that we need to help getting down the stairs') and the fridge decline both land with no empathy and no use of her name after the greeting.
audio_review_reason: The transcript has clear alignment defects — Dustin's 'Perfect' appears inside his own opening before Leslie answers, and her replies stack as three consecutive 'Yes' lines — so tone cannot be judged reliably at the two moments that matter most: the 'we wouldn't be a good fit for this project' disqualification, and whether Leslie actually confirmed the ten-box assumption or just gave a passing 'Mm-hmm.'
